title: Arjuna's Despair and Collapse
story:
The two armies had drawn up on the plain of Kurukshetra, and the war everyone had dreaded and prepared for was about to begin. For years the quarrel had been growing — a kingdom lost at a rigged game of dice, a long exile, a peace refused — and now all of it had been folded into this single hour. The men who faced each other were cousins of one royal house: the five Pandava brothers, and the hundred sons of the blind king Dhritarashtra. Every man on that field was someone's father, son, or brother, and almost all of them shared the same blood. Then, before a single arrow flew, the man at the centre of it all lost the will to fight.

The Kauravas and the Pandavas stood facing each other, and the sound of their conches, drums, cymbals, and horns filled the field. Duryodhana had walked the length of his own army with his teacher Drona, naming its champions — Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashwatthaman — and the old grandsire Bhishma, who had watched over both families all his life, had answered with a lion's roar and a blast of his conch. From the Pandava side came the answering thunder: Krishna and Arjuna on their great chariot of white steeds, Bhima, Yudhishthira, the twins, and all the kings of their alliance, each blowing his own great conch until the plain was one vast brazen noise.

And then Arjuna looked across the field, and everything stopped.

He saw the men arrayed before him, his own kinsmen on both sides. There was his grandsire Bhishma, the old warrior who had watched over his whole life. There was Drona, who had taught him the bow. There were Karna and Kripa and Ashwatthaman, and beyond them cousins he had grown up beside, uncles and nephews, the sons of old friends. And behind him, in his own ranks, stood the son of his beloved Subhadra — his own boy — and the sons of Draupadi. These were the men the war had gathered, and these were the men he was asked to kill.

The pity came over him all at once, and it was not a small thing. His body began to tremble, and his hair stood on end, and his skin burned. It was not fear that did this to him; it was something closer to love, and it was stronger than either. The great bow Gandiva, which had never failed him, slipped from his fingers — and with it slipped everything he had prepared for this day. A man who cannot raise his bow cannot fight a war, and this man had been the hope of his whole side.

He spoke to Krishna beside him, and his voice, which had carried across a hundred battlefields, came out low. "I do not wish to kill these men, even if they kill me," he said. What kind of victory, he was asking without quite asking, could be bought with the deaths of his own people?

He did not wait for an answer, or perhaps he could not. His mind heavy with grief, he cast aside his bow and his arrows and sat down in the chariot, there on the field of battle, between two armies that were waiting for him. The conches that had roared a moment before were silent now; the whole field held its breath. The noise of the day fell away, and the man who was supposed to lead them all sat bowed and still.

Krishna did not speak yet. He held the reins and waited — there would be time for words soon. But for now there was only this: the armies hushed on either side, and the strongest man on the field undone not by any enemy, but by the sight of the people he loved standing where he would have to kill them.
reflection: The Gita does not begin with philosophy; it begins with a man falling apart. Before Krishna can teach Arjuna anything, Arjuna has to be honest about what he feels — and what he feels is that the victory he has spent his life preparing for is not worth the faces in front of him.
next_story_tease: But Krishna had not yet spoken — and what he was about to say would become the heart of the teaching.
hero_scene: Arjuna slumped in his chariot on the field of Kurukshetra, the great bow Gandiva slipped from his hand and his arrows cast aside, while Krishna stands quietly at the reins against the hush of two waiting armies.
